source.title: The Dilemma of Quantum Neural Networks
source.authors: Yan Qian; Xin-Biao Wang; Yuxuan Du; Xing-Yao Wu; D. Tao

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure labels and plotted values are garbled in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies random-label fitting experiments to QNNs and DNNs, extending the randomization test cited from Zhang et al. to new models and datasets.
record.gate_note: Tests random-label fitting and generalization on natural-label tasks. Other cited findings are background only. Figure 3 and Figure 4 plotted values are partly garbled; no exact values are reconstructed from them.
record.test_reason: The classical-network experiments repeat the random-label fitting test and measure natural-label train/test accuracy, bearing on V1. The MNIST CNN–MLP experiment also addresses V3, although its relative test accuracies cannot be recovered from the supplied text. Quantum-network results do not directly test the classical-network versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the authors' conclusion: the tested current QNNs have limited effective capacity, underperform classical models on the real-world tasks, receive limited trainability benefits from regularization, and deteriorate under quantum noise. Qualify this by noting that SGD substantially improves optimization, some weight-decay settings help, and QNNs outperform the small MLP on quantum synthetic data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses random-label fitting to assess effective capacity, as in Zhang et al., but evaluates QNNs and DNNs on Wine, a quantum synthetic dataset, and a subset of MNIST rather than the original architectures and datasets.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and model architecture; optimizer and batch size affect QNN training behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: QNNN and QENN fit random labels poorly, with further degradation under simulated quantum noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested quantum circuit classifiers have limited effective memorization capacity.

fits_no_version.finding: CNN exceeds QCNN test accuracy by approximately three percentage points on resized MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The tested classical convolutional model outperforms its quantum convolutional counterpart.

fits_no_version.finding: Batch size affects quantum-model convergence and accuracy; quantum synthetic data have an optimum around batch size 8.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch size influences optimization and held-out performance of the tested quantum classifiers.

record.code_released: The authors state that the related code will be released to the Github repository; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The paper reports means over 10 repetitions but does not provide uncertainty values in the supplied result text. Several relevant plotted values are not recoverable from the flattened figure text, and the MNIST evaluation uses a subset resized to 10 × 10.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were excluded; figure-only values were retained only where the comparison condition was clear, with unrecoverable values marked figure only.

untested.parts: The original CIFAR-10/ImageNet architectures and recipes; readable random-label held-out accuracy; confirmed natural-label generalization of MLP++; and verification that the compared classical training recipes lack explicit regularization.
No test-error trajectory across widths beyond interpolation. Enlarging an MLP to fit random labels does not test this.
The local-connectivity mechanism, learned sparse connections, convolutional initialization, and datasets beyond the resized MNIST subset. The basic CNN–MLP comparison is present but unreadable.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison on the named workloads.
No batch-size comparison for classical image classifiers or language models, including the stated recipe adaptations.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or ranking of generalization gaps.
No influence-based removal of memorized examples and retraining.

missing.what: Separate random-label training-accuracy rows for the small classical CNN and MLP on MNIST. The text explicitly says the small models fail to fit random labels and behave like chance; the ten-class chance baseline is 10%.
missing.locator: Section 3, Figure 4(c) caption and accompanying discussion

missing.what: The enlarged MLP's improved random-label training accuracy on MNIST. The text reports a substantial increase but does not give a recoverable endpoint or establish perfect fitting.

record.verdict_notes: No positive Wine verdict is assigned because the supplied text does not securely establish every part of the coexistence result, especially random-label held-out accuracy. No V3 verdict is justified by the readable CNN–QCNN comparison or the unreadable CNN–MLP ordering. Missing readable values are not evidence of an absent effect.

versions.untested_parts: The specific CIFAR-10 architectures and ImageNet setting in the version are not tested; results cover QNNs and MLPs on the Wine and quantum synthetic datasets, and QNN/CNN/MLP on a subset of MNIST.
The tested image dataset is a subset of MNIST; the paper does not test the stated datasets or the learned sparse connections and convolutional initialization conditions.
Tests batch size in QNNs on Wine and quantum synthetic data, not the stated image-classification or language-model settings, fixed epoch comparison, or adaptation strategies.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.size_stated: For Wine, number of trainable parameters kept close to QNNs; exact count not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Wine with random labels for 40 epochs.
rows.note: The paper states MLP reaches perfect training accuracy on Wine with random labels.
rows.check: Correct as the random-label memorization component: MLP reaches 100% training accuracy on binary Wine after 40 epochs. This row alone does not establish generalization.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.size_stated: For Wine, number of trainable parameters kept close to QNNs; exact count not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Wine with natural labels.
rows.note: The text says MLP outperforms QNNs by 10% to 20% on Wine, but gives no exact MLP test accuracy.
rows.check: The exact natural-label test accuracy is unreadable. Section 3 reports favorable natural-label performance, but the reported 10–20 percentage-point advantage over QNNs is not itself an accuracy relative to the 50% chance baseline.

rows.subject: QNNN
rows.size_stated: 13 qubits for the Wine dataset; exact trainable parameter count not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Wine with random labels.
rows.note: The authors describe this as only slightly better than random guess.
rows.check: QNNN is a quantum circuit model, outside V1's classical architectures. The prose reports 0.562 but does not explicitly attach that number to Wine rather than the quantum-data panel.

rows.subject: QENN
rows.size_stated: 13 qubits for the Wine dataset; exact trainable parameter count not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on Wine with random labels.
rows.note: The authors describe this as only slightly better than random guess.
rows.check: QENN is a quantum circuit model, outside V1's classical architectures. The prose reports 0.630 but does not explicitly attach that number to Wine rather than the quantum-data panel.

rows.subject: MLP++
rows.size_stated: Larger-scale MLP; exact size not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on quantum synthetic data with random labels.
rows.note: Quantum synthetic data are not natural-label data, so this row does not establish the natural-label part of V1.
rows.check: Valid evidence for the random-label fitting component only. Matching natural-label generalization for this enlarged MLP is not reported; the quantum-generated task is also outside the natural-label benchmarks in V1.

rows.subject: MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a subset of MNIST with natural labels.
rows.note: The paper compares this fully connected model with QCNN and CNN, but the supplied figure text does not recover its exact accuracy.
rows.check: The MLP is the relevant fully connected comparator, but its test accuracy and its ordering against CNN cannot be recovered. MNIST is a dataset named by V3; the restrictions are resizing and the small subset.

source_check.correct: MNIST MLP test accuracy is figure-only; no explicit random-guess baseline is stated for this comparison. The natural-label MLP test accuracy described as chance-like concerns the quantum synthetic dataset.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Figure 3(c) and accompanying paragraphs, lines 501–531; Appendix C.2, lines 1625–1629.
source_check.problem: The random-guess comparison in the accompanying text belongs to the quantum synthetic dataset, not MNIST.

rows.subject: CNN
rows.size_stated: Same overall structure as QCNN; exact parameter count not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a subset of MNIST with natural labels.
rows.note: The paper says QCNN reaches 93% accuracy on both train and test sets and is approximately 3% worse than CNN.
rows.check: CNN test accuracy is approximately 96%, inferred from QCNN's 93% and the stated three-point difference. For V3 the required baseline is MLP, whose accuracy is unreadable. CNN outperforming QCNN does not establish CNN outperforming a fully connected network.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3, Figure 3(c), lines 527–531; Appendix C.2, lines 1622–1624.

rows.baseline: best batch size around 8 in this setting

rows.check: Quantum classifiers on quantum synthetic data are outside V5. Figure 13(b) does measure test accuracy, and the prose identifies a nonmonotonic decline with an optimum around batch size 8, but this cannot establish V5 for its named systems.

relationships.condition: Small classical CNN and MLP on 2,000 resized MNIST training images
relationships.reason: Section 3 and Figure 4(c) explicitly report chance-like random-label fitting for the small models. This qualifies extension of V1 to these architectures; the result is missing from the rows.
relationships.display_finding: The available source does not verify the report that training performance on random labels was near chance. It also does not establish whether the failure to fit them persists with longer training.
